Findings.Comment: The retry classification is inverted relative to the previous code and to `Deliver`'s own doc comment ("a transient failure is retried ... a permanent one is returned at once"). Previously the guard was `if !retryable(err) { return err }`, so permanent errors short-circuited and transient ones fell through to the backoff loop. With `if retryable(lastErr) { return lastErr }`, a transient failure (e.g. HTTP 503 from `post`) is now returned to the caller after a single attempt, while a permanent rejection (e.g. HTTP 404 wrapping `ErrPermanent`) burns all `maxAttempts` retries with backoff before the "giving up" error is produced — exactly the opposite of the documented contract.

Findings.Comment: The `defer resp.Body.Close()` that previously followed the `c.http.Do(req)` error check is gone, and nothing else in `WhoAmI` closes `resp.Body` (the function returns `*User`, so a caller cannot close it either). On every call — success, non-2xx status, or decode failure — the response body is left open, so the underlying connection is never released back to the `http.Transport` pool. Under any sustained call rate this exhausts sockets/file descriptors and stalls requests once the pool limit is reached.

Findings.Comment: The `defer resp.Body.Close()` that used to follow `c.http.Do(req)` is gone and nothing else in `WhoAmI` closes the body. On any call — the non-2xx early return at the status check, the decode error path, or the success path — `resp.Body` is left open, so the underlying connection can never be returned to the transport's idle pool and the file descriptor stays pinned until finalization. A caller invoking `WhoAmI` on a hot path (e.g. per-token validation) will accumulate open connections and can exhaust fds or stall subsequent requests.

Every successful call decodes the body and returns `*User` with no handle on the response left for the caller, so the connection is never released back to the pool; a loop of lookups (e.g. validating a batch of tokens) leaks one idle connection per call and eventually starves `http.Transport`. Repeated `WhoAmI` calls will not return connections to the keep-alive pool, eventually exhausting file descriptors or hanging requests.
Findings.Headline: Response body never closed in WhoAmI after removing the defer

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: This change drops the only `resp.Body.Close()` in `WhoAmI`, and the function returns just `(*User, error)`, so no caller can close the body either. On every request — success or non-2xx — the response body is read but never closed, which in `net/http` prevents the underlying connection from being returned to the keep-alive pool and leaks it. Repeated `WhoAmI` calls (e.g. per-request auth checks) will accumulate open connections until the file descriptor limit or server-side timeouts bite.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI no longer closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: The mutex around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` was removed, leaving the worker writing `q.depth` (and reading `q.pending`) with no lock held. `Submit` and `Depth` both access those fields under `q.mu`, so as soon as a caller submits a job while the worker finishes `q.run(j)`, two goroutines touch `q.depth` concurrently. In Go that is a data race: the race detector will flag it, and `Depth()` can report a torn/stale backlog count. The pre-diff code guarded this exact assignment for that reason.
Findings.Headline: Worker updates q.depth without holding the mutex

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The mutex lock/unlock around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` was removed, so the worker now writes `depth` with no synchronization while `Submit` and `Depth` read and write the same field under `q.mu`. On any run where a `Submit` arrives while a job is finishing (or a `Depth()` call lands between `q.run(j)` and the update), the concurrent unsynchronized write races with the mutex-protected accesses — this is undefined behavior in Go, produces stale/incorrect backlog counts, and will fail under the race detector.
Findings.Headline: Worker updates Queue.depth without holding the mutex

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: `worker` updates the backlog count after each job with no lock held, while `Submit` appends to `q.pending` under `q.mu` and `Depth` reads `q.depth` under `q.mu`. In any run where a job completes concurrently with a `Submit` (or with a `Depth` poll — both realistic for a queue that "never blocks"), the unlocked `len(q.pending)` read races with the append and the unlocked `q.depth` write races with the locked read, so `Depth()` can report a stale value and the Go race detector aborts the process in race builds. Restore the mutex around the update, or fold the update into `take()` so it happens under the same critical section that mutates `q.pending`.
Findings.Headline: Unlocked write to q.depth in worker races with Submit and Depth

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The mutex guards around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` were dropped, but `Depth()` still reads `q.depth` under `q.mu` and `Submit` writes it under `q.mu`. With one goroutine submitting jobs while `worker` drains the queue (the exact scenario this type exists for), the worker's unlocked write and `len(q.pending)` read race against `Submit`'s `append` and depth update — a data race on both the `depth` int and the `pending` slice header, yielding undefined behavior under the Go memory model and a guaranteed failure under the race detector. The write must be performed under the same lock the readers use.
Findings.Headline: Unlocked write to shared depth in worker is a data race

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: Dropping the lock around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` in `worker` makes this write race with the mutex-protected readers/writers of the same field. On a realistic path, the worker goroutine finishes `q.run(j)` and updates the depth while a caller concurrently runs `Submit` (which appends to `q.pending` and writes `q.depth` under the mutex) or calls `Depth()` (which reads `q.depth` under the mutex). Since the worker's write is now unsynchronized, the Go memory model gives no ordering guarantees: `Depth()` can report a stale or torn value, the unsynchronized `len(q.pending)` read can observe a partially updated slice header, and `-race` builds will report a data race between `worker` and `Submit`/`Depth`.
Findings.Headline: Unsynchronized write to q.depth in worker races with Submit and Depth

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The try/catch around `return this.refresh(base)` never fires for the failure it is written for. `refresh` is `async`, so `this.provider.fetch(base)` rejecting produces a rejected promise rather than a synchronous throw; `return <promise>` completes the `try` block normally and the rejection propagates straight to the caller. On the realistic path (network/HTTP failure, which rejects asynchronously) `getRates` still rejects, `staleServed` is never incremented, and the expired table is never served — so the fallback documented in the method comment above does not actually work. The catch only triggers on a synchronous throw from `provider.fetch`, `cache.set`, or the logger, which is not how async providers fail.
Findings.Headline: Stale-rate fallback never runs: async rejection bypasses try/catch

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The new fallback path in `getRates` never runs. `refresh(base)` returns a promise, and `return this.refresh(base)` inside a `try` without `await` does not route the rejection through the surrounding `catch` — the async function's returned promise simply adopts the rejection. Concretely: cached table is expired → `getRates` enters the `try` → `provider.fetch` rejects → the `catch` block is skipped entirely → the caller receives the provider error instead of the expired table, `staleServed` stays 0, and the new warn log never fires. The whole stale-serving feature is unreachable; it needs `return await` (or awaiting into a local before returning) so the `catch` actually observes the rejection.
Findings.Headline: Un-awaited return skips the catch; stale-table fallback never triggers

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The `try`/`catch` around `return this.refresh(base)` never catches a rejected provider call: `refresh` returns a promise that is not awaited inside the `try` block, so a rejection propagates straight to the caller and the `catch` body is unreachable for async failures. When the provider is down and an expired table exists, `getRates` throws instead of serving the cached table, and `staleServed` never increments — defeating the whole point of this change. Awaiting the returned promise inside the `try` makes the fallback actually run.
Findings.Headline: Stale-cache fallback never runs: refresh promise is returned unawaited

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `refresh` is `async`, so a provider failure surfaces as a rejected promise rather than a synchronous throw. Because `getRates` returns `this.refresh(base)` without awaiting it, the `try`/`catch` never sees that rejection — the promise is returned as-is and its rejection propagates straight to the caller. On exactly the path this change targets (an expired cached table plus a failing provider), the request still fails, `staleServed` is never incremented, no warning is logged, and the expired table is never served. The `catch` block is effectively dead code unless `refresh` throws before its first `await`, which cannot happen for an `async` method. Awaiting the call inside the `try` makes the rejection throw at the `return` statement and reach the fallback.
Findings.Headline: Un-awaited return makes the stale-rate fallback catch unreachable

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The catch block never runs on provider failure because the rejected promise is returned, not awaited. In an async function, `return this.refresh(base)` adopts the promise without letting the surrounding `try` observe its rejection — the rejection propagates straight to the caller. Concretely: cache holds an expired table, `provider.fetch` rejects → `getRates` rejects instead of serving `cached`, so the stale-table fallback, the `staleServed` counter, and the `logger.warn` never execute. This is the classic missing-`await`-in-`try` pitfall and makes the entire fallback feature dead code.
Findings.Headline: Missing await in try/catch makes stale-rate fallback unreachable

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `tx.Commit(ctx)` discards its error, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success. If the commit fails (connection dropped mid-commit, serialization/deferred-constraint failure, context cancellation between Exec and Commit), `AddClaim` returns nil while the claim row is never persisted, and the deferred `tx.Rollback` on an already-closed tx is a no-op. The caller has no way to know the write was lost, which is silent data loss on a realistic path. Restore the commit error check that this hunk removed.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim drops the tx.Commit error and reports success on failed commits

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: `AddClaim` previously wrapped and returned the commit error; now `tx.Commit(ctx)`'s return value is discarded and the function always returns `nil` on this path. A commit can fail on deferred constraint checks, serialization failure, or a dropped connection between the INSERT and the commit — in each case the caller is told the claim was recorded while `team_claims` has no row, so the claim silently disappears. Callers that treat `nil` as "ownership recorded" will proceed as if the team owns the project.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim discards tx.Commit error and reports success unconditionally

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: `AddClaim` now discards the result of `tx.Commit(ctx)` and returns `nil` unconditionally. If the commit fails (serialization failure, connection drop, constraint violation deferred to commit time), the caller is told the team claim was recorded while `team_claims` contains no row. Any caller that treats a nil return as a durable claim will proceed on wrong state, and the deferred `tx.Rollback` on an already-closed transaction is a no-op, so the failure is silently swallowed with no error surfaced anywhere.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim swallows commit errors and reports false success

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: `AddClaim` now discards the error returned by `tx.Commit(ctx)` and unconditionally returns `nil`. If the commit fails (serialization failure, constraint violation deferred to commit time, connection drop, context cancellation), the caller is told the claim was recorded when it was not — a team can believe it owns a project while `team_claims` has no row, and no retry or log line ever surfaces the failure. The previous code wrapped and returned the commit error; restoring that check keeps the transaction's failure visible to callers.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim swallows tx.Commit error and reports success on failed writes

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: Ignoring the error from `tx.Commit(ctx)` means a failed commit is reported as success. `AddClaim` writes the claim and then commits; if that commit fails — e.g. the connection drops after the INSERT, or the transaction is rolled back by the server — the row is not durably recorded, yet `AddClaim` returns `nil`. Callers then treat the team as owning the project and proceed on a claim that was never persisted, which is silent data loss. The removed code explicitly checked this error and wrapped it; that check needs to stay.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim drops the commit error and reports failed commits as success

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error branches are inverted relative to the documented contract on `ErrNoClaim` ("what callers match on when a project has no owner yet", distinguished from a database fault with `errors.Is`). After this change, a `no rows` result — the actual "nobody owns it" case — is wrapped around `errNoRows` (pgx's sentinel), so `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNoClaim)` is false and callers fall through to the database-fault path. Conversely, a genuine connection failure wraps `ErrNoClaim`, so callers treat a broken DB as "project is unowned" and may let a team claim it or surface a misleading empty owner. Any caller following the documented `errors.Is` contract breaks on every call.
Findings.Headline: ErrNoClaim wraps database faults; no-rows case no longer reports ErrNoClaim

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two error-wrapping branches are swapped. On a database fault (connection error, timeout, permission failure) `Scan` returns a non-`errNoRows` error, so the `if err != nil` branch fires and returns `ErrNoClaim` — callers matching on `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will treat an outage as "nobody owns this project". Conversely, the genuine no-owner case now returns the raw `errNoRows` wrapped, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false exactly when the claim is missing. This inverts the contract stated directly above: `ErrNoClaim is what callers match on when a project has no owner yet` and `Callers distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with errors.Is.` Callers that act on the no-claim path will proceed to claim a project during a transient DB failure.
Findings.Headline: Error wrapping swapped between no-claim and database-fault branches

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two error paths are swapped relative to the documented contract. On the no-rows path (`errors.Is(err, errNoRows)`), the raw `err` is now wrapped instead of `ErrNoClaim`, so a caller doing `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNoClaim)` for an unclaimed project returns false and will treat "no owner" as a database fault. Conversely, on the catch-all `if err != nil` branch (real DB/connection failures), `ErrNoClaim` is wrapped, so a genuine database fault is misreported as "nobody owns this project" and callers that auto-claim on `ErrNoClaim` will silently claim projects during outages. This directly contradicts the package comment "ErrNoClaim is what callers match on when a project has no owner yet" and the `Owner` doc "Callers distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault with errors.Is.".
Findings.Headline: Owner swaps ErrNoClaim and raw err between the two error paths

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two `return` branches were swapped, inverting the error contract of `Owner`. On a missing row (`errors.Is(err, errNoRows)`) the function now wraps the raw `err` instead of `ErrNoClaim`, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false exactly when the project has nobody owning it — contradicting the doc comment two lines above, which promises callers can distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with `errors.Is`. Conversely, a genuine database fault is now reported as `ErrNoClaim`, so a caller that re-claims unowned projects would treat an outage/permission error as "free to claim" and can overwrite another team's claim. Any caller written to the documented contract breaks on both paths.
Findings.Headline: ErrNoClaim and raw error wrapping swapped in Owner

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two branches now wrap the opposite errors from the documented contract in the comment above (`Callers distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with errors.Is`). On `errNoRows` (nobody owns the project) the returned error wraps the raw driver error, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false; on any other database fault (connection dropped, timeout, permission denied) the returned error wraps `ErrNoClaim`, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is true. A caller that uses `ErrNoClaim` to decide whether it is safe to assign an owner will therefore treat a transient DB failure as "no owner" and may claim/overwrite a project that already has an owner, while genuine "no owner" results fall through to the fault-handling path (retries, 500s).
Findings.Headline: Store.Owner wraps ErrNoClaim on DB faults and the raw error on no-rows

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
